thread.title: Goldwater Institute sues Phoenix over public records for $450M Suns arena renovations

title: Goldwater Institute sues Phoenix over public records for $450M Suns arena renovations
text: Order Reprints May 1, 2018, 9:54pm MST The Goldwater Institute and Phoenix attorney Alexander Kolodin are suing the city of Phoenix over public records related to planned $450 million renovations of Talking Stick Resort Arena. The lawsuit centers around non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) struck between cities and other governments and sports teams as well as businesses and real estate developers. NDAs are essentially gag rules that keep public officials from talking and public records from being released. The city is in negotiations with the National Basketball Association’s Phoenix Suns over modernizing the city-owned downtown arena. The lawsuit was filed in Maricopa Superior Court Tuesday and comes after the city denied an arena public records request. Goldwater attorney Jonathan Riches said the watchdog group could look at challenging NDAs related to sports deals in other states as well as NDAs in economic development deals. Big companies such as Amazon.com (Nasdaq: AMZN) and Apple (Nasdaq: AAPL) often require public economic development and elected officials to sign non-disclosure agreements during site selection processes. “You can’t sign away the public’s right to know,” said Riches of NDAs involving sports deals such as the Suns as well as economic development deals. Julie Watters , the city’s communications director, said Phoenix denied the previous public records request that sparked the new lawsuit. “The city temporarily has withheld the Suns’ conceptual design and construction documents regarding a renovation of Talking Stick Resort Arena,” Watters said. Watters said Arizona law protects documents in the middle of procurement and the negotiation process from being made public before a final contract is awarded. “At least for now, disclosing these documents could prevent the city from receiving the best price for the work outlined in those documents,” she said. Watters said when the city’s negotiations with the Suns conclude the information will be made public. Riches and Kolodin question where the city and Suns are in the arena negotiations. Riches said Arizona public records laws side on the public’s right to know. May 1, 2018, 9:54pm MST Related Content
